title: 'All the Hill Country of Judah': From a Settlement Fringe to a Prosperous Monarchy
author: Avi Ofer
publisher: Israel Exploration Society / Yad Izhak Ben-Zvi (in From Nomadism to Monarchy: Archaeological and Historical Aspects of Early Israel, eds. Israel Finkelstein and Nadav Na'aman)
allowedUseNotes: Copyrighted scholarly book chapter. Project stores its own summary of the site-survey conclusions only; no reproduction of maps, plans, or pottery drawings.
summary: Synthesis of the Judean Hills Survey Expedition (Tel Aviv University, directed by Avi Ofer, 1980s field seasons at and around Tell Rumeida/Hebron, drawing on Ofer's 1993 doctoral dissertation) on Iron Age settlement in the Judean highlands. For Hebron specifically, Ofer's survey/excavation work found that the Middle Bronze Age 'cyclopean' perimeter wall on Tell Rumeida was reused during Iron Age I (11th-10th centuries BCE), and reads this as the site's occupational peak, spanning roughly the 11th century into the end of the 10th century BCE. Distinct Iron IIA-specific (10th-9th century) remains at the site, as opposed to this broader Iron I-into-early-Iron-II horizon, are reported as comparatively few and scattered, not a well-defined separate stratum or building plan.
confidenceNotes: TO VERIFY: bibliographic details (exact chapter title, publisher, page range) assembled from secondary/tertiary search-result summaries (a TheTorah.com article and other secondary discussions citing Ofer), not from direct inspection of the 1994 volume itself or Ofer's 1993 Tel Aviv University dissertation. The reused-cyclopean-wall reading is now itself disputed by more recent scholarship redating that same wall to the later Iron Age (see ussishkin-2021-cyclopean-wall-hebron, a 2021 reassessment) — this card's summary should be read as Ofer's 1994 position specifically, not as the settled current consensus. Supports only a general 'reused massive perimeter wall, occupational peak in this era' picture for claim-hebron-town-form, not any specific gate, building footprint, or town plan.
